Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts

leap year noun

also leap day

classical

Plin. NH 18.207: annō intercalāriō
Plin. NH 2.130

annus intercalārius

Pliny’s term for the year with the added day. Caesar fixed the year at 365 days, adding a day every fourth year (Suet. Jul. 40.1). The Romans did not add a 29 February: they counted the sixth day before the Kalends of March twice, whence late Latin bisextus, the leap day.

Other words

  • diēs intercalārius — the leap day

    also used · classical · Plin. NH 2.35: ūnus intercalārius diēs additur; Traupman 78–79: ante diem bis VI Kalendās Mārtiās

  • annus bisextilis — leap year

    also used · late Latin · Isid. Orig. 6.17.25 (Lewis & Short)

    The medieval and Church term, from bisextus, the leap day (Censorinus, Ammianus; Lewis & Short, who call the spelling bissextus an error).

Examples

  • ūnus diēs quārtō quōque annō intercalārētur

    (Caesar arranged that) one day should be added every fourth yearSuet. Jul. 40.1

  • quam ob causam quīntō annō ūnus intercalārius diēs additur

    for this reason an extra day is added every fourth year (“in the fifth year”, counting both ends)Plin. NH 2.35

See also February, calendar, the Kalends.
